t:
Subsection (d) of section 2 of the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956 (12 U.S.C. 1841(d)) is amended to read as follows:


“(d) 
‘Subsidiary’, with respect to a specified bank holding company, means (1) any company 25 per centum or more of whose voting shares (excluding shares owned by the United States or by any company wholly owned by the United States) is directly or indirectly owned or controlled by such bank holding company, or is held by it with power to vote; or (2) any company the election of a majority of whose directors is controlled in any manner by such bank holding company.”

fable.w: This section only amends the statutory definition of 'Subsidiary' in the Bank Holding Company Act, based on share ownership or control of director elections. The tempting reading is that the mention of 'election' of directors or 'voting shares' signals participation, but these refer to corporate governance inside private companies, not outside parties being consulted on a federal decision. The section contains no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation, rulemaking authority, or right to sue.
fable.s: any company the election of a majority of whose directors is controlled in any manner by such bank holding company

qwen_block.w: This section provides a statutory definition of the term 'Subsidiary' for the purposes of the Bank Holding Company Act. It describes ownership thresholds and control mechanisms but does not establish any process for public comment, consultation with outside entities, advisory boards, or hearings. It is purely definitional text.
qwen_block.s: “Subsidiary’, with respect to a specified bank holding company, means (1) any company 25 per centum or more of whose voting shares (excluding shares owned by the United States or by any company wholly owned by the United States) is directly or indirectly owned or controlled by such bank holding company, or is held by it with power to vote; or (2) any company the election of a majority of whose directors is controlled in any manner by such bank holding company.”

opus.w: This section only rewrites the definition of "Subsidiary" in the Bank Holding Company Act. One could misread "power to vote" and "election of a majority of whose directors" as a participation process. Those phrases describe how a company is controlled through its shares. They have nothing to do with outsiders taking part in a federal decision. The section creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation, or right to sue, so the answer is No.

qwen_chat.w: This section provides a legal definition of the term 'subsidiary' for the purposes of the Bank Holding Company Act. It does not require or recommend any consultation, coordination, or participation by outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) in a federal decision-making process. It is a substantive definition of corporate control, not a procedural mechanism for public input.
qwen_chat.s: “Subsidiary’, with respect to a specified bank holding company, means (1) any company 25 per centum or more of whose voting shares (excluding shares owned by the United States or by any company wholly owned by the United States) is directly or indirectly owned or controlled by such bank holding company, or is held by it with power to vote; or (2) any company the election of a majority of whose directors is controlled in any manner by such bank holding company.”
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that defining "subsidiary" involves the public or companies, but this is merely a statutory definition for regulatory purposes. It does not establish a process for outside parties to consult with, advise, or participate in a federal decision. The text is purely definitional and procedural regarding ownership thresholds.
